topic.title: Changing the subject with powers, roots, or the subject appearing twice
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: M7 and M8 are each two 75-minute papers of 50 marks: Paper 1 non-calculator, Paper 2 calculator. Changing the subject is set in nearly every series and in both units — in summer 2025 the identical formula appeared as M7 Paper 2 Q13 and as M8 Paper 2 Q6. It is almost always a single part with no context: the formula is printed on its own line and the answer line already reads 'Answer x =', which tells you the examiner wants the letter isolated. Two marks is the standard tariff for one or two clean steps (November 2024 M8 Paper 1 Q9, summer 2023 M7 Paper 2 Q10(b), summer 2026 M7 Paper 1 Q11 and M8 Paper 1 Q2, November 2023 M7 Paper 2 Q15). Three marks is the tariff whenever the subject appears twice or a power has to be undone (summer 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q13 and M8 Paper 2 Q6, summer 2022 M7 Paper 1 Q14 and M8 Paper 1 Q8). Position is late: question 13 to 17 of an M7 paper, and anywhere from question 2 to question 9 of M8, where the paper starts harder. Schemes run one MA1 per rearrangement line — collected line, factorised line, finished subject — or MA1 then A1 on a two-mark part, so a part-finished script still scores.

Undo the operations in reverse order: the last thing done to the subject is the first thing off
Subject in two terms: collect, factorise, divide by the whole bracket
Clear a denominator first, multiplying every term on both sides
Isolate the power completely, then root the whole side; write ± unless the context rules the negative out
A = πr² gives r = √(A/π), and V = ⅓πr²h gives r = √(3V/πh)
notOnThisSpec: Rearranging a formula that needs the quadratic formula, for example making r the subject of A = 2πr² + 2πrh — M7-NA-07 covers a power OR the subject in more than one term, and no paper read sets both at once in a way that produces a quadratic in the subject
Changing the subject of a formula containing a logarithm, an exponential or a trigonometric function — A level
Functions and inverse functions, f⁻¹(x) — not on this specification, although the reverse-the-operations chain here is exactly the idea it becomes

Proving that a rearrangement is valid for every value, or stating the values the letters may not take (division by zero) — beyond GCSE, though it is worth noticing that the bracket you divide by must not be zero

sheet.howExamined: M7 and M8 are each two 75-minute papers of 50 marks: Paper 1 non-calculator, Paper 2 calculator. Three marks is the tariff whenever the subject appears twice or a power has to be undone (summer 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q13 and M8 Paper 2 Q6, summer 2022 M7 Paper 1 Q14 and M8 Paper 1 Q8). traps: Leaving the subject on both sides: over a third of the M8 entry never gathered the terms together, which is what the first mark is for (summer 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q6)
Collecting the terms and then stopping, because the subject was never factorised out of them (summer 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q13)
Taking the square root before the squared term has been isolated, so the division is trapped under the root (November 2024 M7 Paper 1 Q17)
Drawing the root over the numerator only instead of over the whole side (November 2024 M7 Paper 1 Q17)
Failing the plainest step of all — over a fifth could not divide both sides by a single letter (November 2024 M8 Paper 1 Q9)
Skipping the intermediate line, when a mark was available for that line by itself (summer 2023 M7 Paper 2 Q10)
Dividing by one term of the bracket instead of by the whole bracket, or cancelling a term that is not a factor
Multiplying only some of the terms when clearing a denominator
Losing a sign when a term crosses the equals sign, which the substitution check would catch in thirty seconds
Giving one value where ± was needed, or keeping a negative radius because the reason was never thought about

resources: Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the paper

workedExamples.stem:
The volume of a cone is $V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$, where $r$ is the radius of the base and $h$ is the height.

Make $r$ the subject of the formula.

steps.decision: The $\tfrac{1}{3}$ is a division, and it is the outermost thing in the formula, so it comes off first: multiply the whole of both sides by 3. Clearing the fraction now keeps every line after it free of fractions, which is where sign slips usually come from.

options: Because the division by 3 is the outermost operation, so it is undone first
Because 3 is the smallest number in the formula
Because you always deal with numbers before letters
whyMenu.explain: Size has nothing to do with it. You are undoing a chain, and the chain is undone from the outside in. The $\tfrac{1}{3}$ is wrapped around everything, so it is the first wrapper off.

steps.decision: What is left of the right-hand side is $r^2$ multiplied by $\pi$ and by $h$, so divide both sides by $\pi h$ in a single step. Notice what is now alone: $r^2$, not $r$. That is deliberate — the power always comes off last.

Only now does the square root go on, and it goes over the whole of the other side, fraction and all. A radius cannot be negative, so the negative root is dropped — and that reason is written down rather than assumed.

options: Because the root undoes the square, and it must cover everything the square was applied to
Because roots are always written over fractions
Because the numerator is the only part that was squared
whyMenu.explain: $r^2$ equals the whole fraction, so the root has to act on the whole fraction. Rooting the numerator only gives $\dfrac{\sqrt{3V}}{\pi h}$, which is a different number — this is exactly the slip the November 2024 report describes.

steps.decision: Two lines of arithmetic turn a hopeful answer into a checked one. Pick values that cancel, work the subject out from your rearrangement, then put everything back into the original formula. The two sides agree, so the rearrangement is sound.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: $r = \sqrt{\dfrac{3V}{\pi h}}$, taking the positive root because $r$ is a radius

twin.stem:
Kinetic energy is $E = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, where $v$ is a speed.

Make $v$ the subject of the formula.

resources: Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the paper
Scientific calculator (must be used)

workedExamples.stem:
$8x - 3w = wx + 12$

Make $x$ the subject of this formula.

steps.decision: $x$ appears on both sides, so nothing can be divided yet. The first move is always the same: every term containing $x$ to one side, everything else to the other. The $wx$ crosses and becomes $-wx$; the $-3w$ crosses and becomes $+3w$. This single line is worth a mark on its own, and it is the line a third of the summer 2025 entry never wrote.

options: Because dividing by $x$ now would leave another $x$ behind
Because the left-hand side must always be the longer one
whyMenu.explain: Dividing by $x$ turns $wx$ into $w$ but turns $12$ into $\dfrac{12}{x}$, so the subject is still there. Only when both $x$ terms are side by side can the $x$ be pulled out.

steps.decision: Factorise. Each term on the left gives up its $x$, leaving $8$ and $-w$ inside the bracket, so the subject now appears exactly once in the whole formula. Multiply the bracket back out in your head to check nothing changed.
Divide both sides by the whole bracket $(8 - w)$, not by 8 and not by $-w$. The bracket goes underneath in one piece and the subject is alone.
Both sides of the original formula come to 18, so the rearrangement holds. If they had disagreed you would have caught a sign slip with three marks still in play.

twin.stem:
$5y + 2c = cy + 14$

Make $y$ the subject of the formula.

resources: Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the paper

workedExamples.stem:
$k = \dfrac{2n}{n + 5}$

Make $n$ the subject of the formula.

steps.decision: The subject is inside the denominator, so it cannot move until the fraction is gone. Multiply both sides by $(n+5)$ and expand. Do not be put off that this looks like it has made things worse: it has turned an impossible shape into a familiar one, with $n$ in two terms.

options: Because nothing can be collected while $n$ is trapped underneath a fraction
Because brackets are always expanded first
Because $k$ is the subject at the moment
whyMenu.explain: A denominator is a division wrapped around the whole numerator. Undo it first and every remaining step is ordinary collecting and factorising.

steps.decision: Now it is the standard case. Collect the two $n$ terms on one side, everything else on the other, then factorise $n$ out. Writing both of these on one line is fine as long as both are visible — the CCEA scheme credits the factorised form.
Divide by the whole bracket. The subject is alone on the left and appears nowhere on the right, which is the test for being finished.
The value of $k$ you started with comes back out, so the rearrangement is right. Choosing $k = 1.5$ rather than a whole number was deliberate: it makes an accidental sign flip show up loudly.

twin.stem:
$g = \dfrac{3t}{t - 4}$

Make $t$ the subject of the formula.

resources: Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the paper
Scientific calculator (must be used)

workedExamples.stem:
$T = \dfrac{3x^2}{x^2 + 4}$

Make $x$ the subject of this formula.

steps.decision: This is the hardest shape the specification allows: the subject appears twice and it is squared. Treat $x^2$ as the thing you are making the subject and the whole question becomes the familiar one. Clear the denominator first, as always.

Collect the two $x^2$ terms on one side and the rest on the other. Putting them on the right keeps the coefficient positive, which saves a sign at the end — a small choice, but it is where marks leak.

options: Because both terms contain $x^2$, so they are the ones that must end up together
Because $4T$ is the only term with a number in it
Because the right-hand side is shorter
whyMenu.explain: The rule does not change when the subject is squared: every term containing the thing you want goes to one side. Here that thing is $x^2$.

steps.decision: Factorise $x^2$ out and divide by the whole bracket. The squared subject is now alone, which is the condition for rooting.

Root the whole side. Nothing in the formula says $x$ is a length, so both values survive and the $\pm$ has to be written. Check with $T = 2$: $x^2 = \dfrac{8}{1} = 8$, and putting $x^2 = 8$ back gives $\dfrac{3 \times 8}{8 + 4} = 2$.

twin.stem:
$W = \dfrac{5y^2}{y^2 - 2}$, where $y$ is a positive length.

Make $y$ the subject of the formula.

items.stem: In $y = \dfrac{x}{4} + 9$, which operation do you undo first to make $x$ the subject?

options.feedback: The $+9$ was the last thing done to $x$, so it is the first thing off. That leaves $y - 9 = \dfrac{x}{4}$.
The divide by 4 is wrapped inside the $+9$, so it has to wait. Multiplying by 4 first gives $4y = x + 36$, which is still true but has not undone the chain in order and usually ends in a lost 36.
That would undo a multiplication, and $x$ is being divided by 4, not multiplied. Read the chain before reaching for an operation.
The 9 is added, not multiplied, so it comes off by subtracting. Undoing an addition with a division is the commonest way a two-mark rearrangement scores nothing.

items.stem: $a = b^2 - c$. Which is the finished answer when $b$ is made the subject?
items.skill: Isolate the power, then root the whole side

options.feedback: Add $c$ to both sides to get $b^2 = a + c$, then root the whole of that side. Nothing says $b$ is a length, so both values stay.
The root has been shared out over the two terms. $\sqrt{a+c}$ is not $\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{c}$, and it is certainly not $\sqrt{a} + c$; try $a = 9$, $c = 16$ and the two come to 5 and 7.
Rooting happened before the $-c$ was dealt with. Isolate $b^2$ completely first, then root. This is the error the November 2024 M7 report singles out.
The expression is right and the algebra is sound; only the second value is missing. A squared subject gives two answers, so write $\pm$ unless the context rules one out.

items.skill: Undo a square root by squaring both sides

options.feedback: Square both sides to get $m^2 = n + 7$, then subtract 7. Two clean lines, two marks.
The squaring is right and the sign is not. The 7 is added to $n$ inside the root, so it comes off by subtracting once the root has gone.
Halving is not the opposite of a square root. Squaring is. Halving $\sqrt{16}$ gives 2, but the number under the root was 16.
A second root has been applied instead of a square. The root is already there; your job is to remove it by squaring.

items.stem: $5t = ht + 9$, and $t$ is to be the subject. What is the correct first line?
items.skill: Collect the subject terms on one side

options.feedback: Both $t$ terms are now on the same side, which is what the first mark is for. Next: factorise to $t(5-h) = 9$.
A term has moved, but the wrong one: $t$ is still on both sides, so there is nothing you can divide by. Move the $ht$, not the 9.
Dividing by 5 while $t$ is still on the right means $t$ has not been made the subject at all. The examiner reads the right-hand side, sees a $t$ and awards nothing.
The $ht$ crossed the equals sign but kept its sign. Moving a positive term makes it negative: $5t - ht = 9$.

items.stem: You have reached $x(4 - p) = 7$. What finishes the rearrangement?

options.feedback: The bracket is one factor, so it moves underneath in one piece: $x = \dfrac{7}{4 - p}$.

options.text: Divide both sides by 4, then by $-p$
options.feedback: The bracket is a single factor, not two separate ones. Dividing by 4 alone does nothing useful, because 4 is added to $-p$ inside the bracket rather than multiplying it.

options.text: Expand the bracket to get $4x - px = 7$
options.feedback: That is true, but it undoes the work: you have just put the subject back into two terms. Factorising was the step before the finish, not a detour.
The 4 is inside a bracket that multiplies $x$, so it cannot be taken off the outside. Only the whole bracket can move, and it moves by division.

items.stem: Which statement about square roots is true?
items.skill: A root acts on the whole side, not term by term

options.text: $\sqrt{u + v}$ is not the same as $\sqrt{u} + \sqrt{v}$
options.feedback: Correct, and it is worth testing once so you never forget: $\sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$ while $\sqrt{9} + \sqrt{16} = 7$.
Roots do not share out over a sum. Try $u = 9$ and $v = 16$: one side is 5, the other is 7.
Halving is not rooting. $\sqrt{16}$ is 4 and half of 16 is 8. The confusion comes from the 2 in the phrase 'square root'.

options.text: Rooting both sides of $u = v^2 + 3$ gives $\sqrt{u} = v + \sqrt{3}$
options.feedback: Same slip inside a rearrangement. Subtract the 3 first, then root: $v = \sqrt{u - 3}$.

items.stem: $y = \dfrac{3w + 1}{5}$, and $w$ is to be the subject. What is the first move?
items.skill: Clear the denominator before anything else

options.feedback: The whole of $3w + 1$ is being divided by 5, so undo that first: $5y = 3w + 1$.
The 1 is inside the fraction, so it is not yet available to move. Clear the denominator and it comes within reach on the next line.

options.text: Multiply the left-hand side by 5 and leave the right alone
options.feedback: That tips the balance. Whatever is done to one side must be done to the whole of the other.
The 3 multiplies $w$ inside the fraction, so it is the last thing to be undone, not the first.

items.stem: You reach $x^2 = \dfrac{9k}{4}$ in a question that says 'Work out the values of $x$'. What goes on the answer line?
items.skill: Decide when a rearranged square needs both values

options.feedback: Values, plural, and nothing here is a length, so both survive. Rooting top and bottom of the fraction gives $\dfrac{3\sqrt{k}}{2}$.
The arithmetic is right; the answer line is short by one value. Drop the negative only when you can write the reason beside it.
The square has been undone by halving. Root the numerator and the denominator instead: $\sqrt{9k} = 3\sqrt{k}$ and $\sqrt{4} = 2$.
The root reached the numerator but stopped before the denominator. It has to cover the whole of that side, so the 4 becomes 2.

parts.stem:
$y = 5x - 8$

Make $x$ the subject of this formula.
hints: What is the last thing done to $x$ when you work $y$ out? Undo that first.
Add 8 to both sides before you divide by anything.
The whole of $y + 8$ goes over the 5, so keep it together.
parts.workedSolution: The chain on $x$ is: multiply by 5, then subtract 8. Undo it backwards. Add 8 to both sides: $y + 8 = 5x$. Divide both sides by 5: $x = \dfrac{y+8}{5}$. Check with $x = 4$: $y = 12$, and $\dfrac{12+8}{5} = 4$.

commonErrors.feedback: The 8 kept its sign as it crossed the equals sign. It is being subtracted on the right, so it is added on the left: $y + 8 = 5x$. Substituting $x = 4$ into both versions would have shown this in ten seconds.
The division by 5 happened before the 8 was moved, so only part of the left-hand side got divided. Undo the $-8$ first, then divide the whole of $y + 8$ by 5.

parts.stem:
$y = \dfrac{x}{3} + 4$

Make $x$ the subject of this formula.
hints: The $+4$ is outside the fraction, so it comes off first.
Then multiply both sides by 3 — all of the left-hand side, not just part of it.
$3(y-4)$ and $3y - 12$ are the same answer.
parts.workedSolution: Subtract 4 from both sides: $y - 4 = \dfrac{x}{3}$. Multiply both sides by 3: $3(y-4) = x$, so $x = 3y - 12$. Check with $x = 9$: $y = 7$, and $3(7-4) = 9$.

commonErrors.feedback: Multiplying by 3 has to reach every term on that side. $3(y-4)$ is $3y - 12$, not $3y - 4$. Writing the bracket first is the safest habit.
$x$ is being divided by 3 in the formula, so it is undone by multiplying, not by dividing again. Reading the chain forwards first — divide by 3, then add 4 — makes the reverse obvious.

parts.stem:
$y = \dfrac{x - 6}{7}$

Make $x$ the subject of this formula.
hints: The whole of $x - 6$ is being divided by 7, so multiply both sides by 7 first.
That gives $7y = x - 6$.
Now add 6 to both sides.
parts.workedSolution: Multiply both sides by 7: $7y = x - 6$. Add 6 to both sides: $x = 7y + 6$. Check with $x = 20$: $y = 2$, and $7(2) + 6 = 20$.

commonErrors.feedback: The 6 was added before the fraction had been cleared, so it got multiplied by 7 as well. Clear the denominator first: $7y = x - 6$, then add 6.
The 6 is subtracted on the right, so it is added when it crosses over. Try $x = 20$ in each version and only one gives $y = 2$.

parts.stem:
$y = x^2 - 11$, where $x$ is positive.

Make $x$ the subject of this formula.
hints: Get $x^2$ on its own before you touch the square.
Root the whole of $y + 11$, and the stem has already told you which sign to keep.
parts.workedSolution: Add 11 to both sides: $x^2 = y + 11$. Now the square is alone, so root the whole side: $x = \sqrt{y + 11}$. The stem says $x$ is positive, so the negative root is rejected. Check with $x = 5$: $y = 14$, and $\sqrt{14 + 11} = 5$.

commonErrors.feedback: The root went on before the 11 had been moved, so it covers only part of the side. Isolate $x^2$ first, then root everything that is left. This is the slip the November 2024 M7 report describes.
A square is undone by a square root, not by halving. Halving 25 gives 12.5, but $\sqrt{25}$ is 5.

context.setting: The area of a circle, the formula named in the M7-NA-07 Teacher Guidance

parts.stem:
The area of a circle is $A = \pi r^2$.

Make $r$ the subject of the formula.

scheme.for: $r = \sqrt{\dfrac{A}{\pi}}$ (negative root rejected as $r$ is a radius)

hints: Divide both sides by $\pi$ before rooting anything.
That leaves $r^2$ on its own.
The root goes over the whole fraction, and a radius cannot be negative.
parts.workedSolution: Divide both sides by $\pi$: $\dfrac{A}{\pi} = r^2$. Root the whole of that side: $r = \sqrt{\dfrac{A}{\pi}}$, positive because $r$ is a radius. Check with $r = 3$: $A = 9\pi$, and $\sqrt{\dfrac{9\pi}{\pi}} = 3$.

commonErrors.feedback: The root was taken before the division by $\pi$, so $\pi$ escaped it. Divide first, then root the whole fraction: $\sqrt{\dfrac{A}{\pi}}$.
That is the formula for a circumference rearranged, not an area. The square on $r$ has to be undone by a square root.

questions.solutionProgram: A = pi r^2 => r^2 = A/pi => r = sqrt(A/pi); check r=3: A=9pi, sqrt(9pi/pi)=3

parts.stem:
$y = \sqrt{2x - 1}$

Make $x$ the subject of this formula.
hints: The root is the outermost operation, so square both sides first.
Squaring both sides gives $y^2 = 2x - 1$.
Add 1, then divide the whole of $y^2 + 1$ by 2.
parts.workedSolution: Square both sides: $y^2 = 2x - 1$. Add 1: $y^2 + 1 = 2x$. Divide by 2: $x = \dfrac{y^2+1}{2}$. Check with $x = 13$: $y = \sqrt{25} = 5$, and $\dfrac{25+1}{2} = 13$.

commonErrors.feedback: The 1 is subtracted inside the root, so it is added once the root has gone. Substituting $x = 13$ gives $y = 5$, and this version returns 12 rather than 13.
The root has been moved to the other side instead of removed. Squaring both sides is what clears it: $y^2 = 2x - 1$.

figures.alt: A right-angled triangle. The right angle is at the bottom left. The vertical side is labelled a, the horizontal base is labelled b and the sloping side opposite the right angle is labelled c. The diagram is not drawn accurately.

parts.stem:
The diagram shows a right-angled triangle, so $c^2 = a^2 + b^2$, and $b$ is a length.

Make $b$ the subject of the formula.

scheme.for: $b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2}$ (negative root rejected as $b$ is a length)

hints: Get $b^2$ by itself first by subtracting $a^2$ from both sides.
Root the whole of $c^2 - a^2$ in one go — it does not break into two roots.
parts.workedSolution: Subtract $a^2$ from both sides: $b^2 = c^2 - a^2$. Root the whole of that side: $b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2}$, positive because $b$ is a length. Check with $a = 8$ and $c = 17$: $b = \sqrt{289 - 64} = \sqrt{225} = 15$, and $8^2 + 15^2 = 289 = 17^2$.

commonErrors.feedback: The root has been shared out over the two terms. With $a = 8$ and $c = 17$ that gives 9, but the third side is 15. $\sqrt{c^2 - a^2}$ cannot be simplified to $c - a$.
$a^2$ is added on the right, so it is subtracted when it crosses. As written this makes $b$ the longest side, which the diagram rules out.

parts.stem:
$6x = 2x + w$

Make $x$ the subject of this formula.
hints: $x$ is on both sides, so gather the two $x$ terms first.
Now divide both sides by 4.
parts.workedSolution: Subtract $2x$ from both sides: $4x = w$. Divide by 4: $x = \dfrac{w}{4}$. Here the collecting leaves a plain number in front of $x$, so no bracket is needed. Check with $x = 5$: $w = 30 - 10 = 20$, and $\dfrac{20}{4} = 5$.

commonErrors.feedback: Dividing by 6 before collecting ignores the $2x$ on the right. Take it across first: $6x - 2x = 4x$, so the division at the end is by 4, not by 6.
The $2x$ was added instead of subtracted. It is positive on the right, so it becomes negative when it crosses: $6x - 2x = 4x$.

parts.stem:
$9x - c = cx + 4$

Write down the line of working in which the $x$ terms have been collected and $x$ has been factorised out.
hints: First move every term containing $x$ to the left and everything else to the right.
That gives $9x - cx = 4 + c$.
Now take $x$ outside a bracket.
parts.workedSolution: Collecting gives $9x - cx = 4 + c$. Each term on the left contains $x$, so it comes out of both: $x(9-c) = 4+c$. Expanding the bracket in your head returns $9x - cx$, so nothing has changed in value.

commonErrors.feedback: The terms are collected, which is the first mark, but the $x$ has not been taken outside a bracket yet. That factorised line is the second mark, and it is the one the summer 2025 report says most scripts never reached.
The $cx$ is positive on the right, so it becomes negative when it moves: the bracket is $(9 - c)$, not $(9 + c)$.

parts.stem: Make $x$ the subject of this formula.

scheme.for: divides both sides by the whole bracket $(9-c)$

hints: Start from your factorised line.
The bracket is a single factor, so it moves underneath in one piece.
parts.workedSolution: From $x(9-c) = 4+c$, divide both sides by $(9-c)$: $x = \dfrac{4+c}{9-c}$. Check with $c = 1$: $x = \dfrac{5}{8}$, and $9\left(\dfrac{5}{8}\right) - 1 = 4.625$ while $1\left(\dfrac{5}{8}\right) + 4 = 4.625$.

commonErrors.feedback: Only the 9 was divided out, so the $-cx$ was left behind. The bracket $(9-c)$ is one factor and the whole of it goes underneath.
The $c$ on the left is subtracted, so it becomes $+c$ on the right. Only the numerator is affected; the bracket underneath is right.

resources: Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the paper

parts.stem:
$ax + 3 = 5x - b$

Make $x$ the subject of this formula.
hints: Both $x$ terms move to one side; choosing the side with $5x$ keeps the bracket positive.
Factorise $x$ out, then divide by the whole bracket.
parts.workedSolution: Move $ax$ right and $-b$ left: $b + 3 = 5x - ax$. Factorise: $b + 3 = x(5-a)$. Divide by $(5-a)$: $x = \dfrac{b+3}{5-a}$. Check with $a = 2$ and $b = 7$: $x = \dfrac{10}{3}$, and $2\left(\dfrac{10}{3}\right) + 3 = \dfrac{29}{3}$ while $5\left(\dfrac{10}{3}\right) - 7 = \dfrac{29}{3}$.

commonErrors.feedback: The bracket is upside down in sign. Collecting on the right gives $5x - ax = x(5-a)$; collecting on the left gives $x(a-5) = -b-3$, and that minus sign has to be carried into the numerator too.
Dividing by the 5 alone leaves the $ax$ unaccounted for. The whole bracket $(5-a)$ goes underneath.

parts.stem:
$y = \dfrac{4}{x + 2}$

Make $x$ the subject of this formula.
hints: The subject is underneath, so clear the denominator first.
Multiplying both sides by $(x+2)$ gives $y(x+2) = 4$.
Either expand and collect, or divide both sides by $y$ and then subtract 2.
parts.workedSolution: Multiply both sides by $(x+2)$: $y(x+2) = 4$. Divide by $y$: $x + 2 = \dfrac{4}{y}$. Subtract 2: $x = \dfrac{4}{y} - 2 = \dfrac{4-2y}{y}$. Check with $y = 0.5$: $x = \dfrac{4-1}{0.5} = 6$, and $\dfrac{4}{6+2} = 0.5$.

commonErrors.feedback: The 2 is added to $x$ inside the denominator, so it is subtracted when it comes out. Testing $y = 0.5$ gives 10 here, but the formula needs 6.
The 4 has been multiplied by $y$ rather than divided. Multiplying both sides by $(x+2)$ leaves $y(x+2) = 4$, so $y$ ends up underneath the 4, not beside it.

resources: Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the paper

context.setting: Pure algebra, no context; the subject sits above and below the line

parts.stem:
$g = \dfrac{h + 3}{h - 1}$

Make $h$ the subject of the formula.
hints: Clear the denominator first: multiply both sides by $(h-1)$.
Expand, then gather every term containing $h$ on one side.
Factorise $h$ out and divide by the whole bracket.
parts.workedSolution: Multiply both sides by $(h-1)$: $g(h-1) = h+3$, so $gh - g = h + 3$. Collect: $gh - h = 3 + g$. Factorise: $h(g-1) = g+3$. Divide: $h = \dfrac{g+3}{g-1}$. The rearranged formula has the same shape as the original, which is a good sign. Check with $g = 5$: $h = \dfrac{8}{4} = 2$, and $\dfrac{2+3}{2-1} = 5$.

commonErrors.feedback: The collecting is done and it earns its mark, but $h$ is still in two terms. Take it outside a bracket: $h(g-1) = g+3$.
Expanding $g(h-1)$ gives $gh - g$, so the $-g$ moves right and becomes $+g$ in the numerator while the bracket underneath stays $(g-1)$. Only one sign changed; this answer changed the other one.

context.setting: Percentage profit on a sale, the formula named in the M7-NA-07 Teacher Guidance

parts.stem:
A shop works out its percentage profit with $P = \dfrac{100(s - c)}{c}$, where $c$ is the cost price and $s$ is the selling price.

Make $s$ the subject of the formula.
hints: Multiply both sides by $c$ to clear the fraction.
Expand the bracket so the $s$ term is free: $Pc = 100s - 100c$.
Move the $100c$ across, then divide the whole side by 100.
parts.workedSolution: Multiply both sides by $c$: $Pc = 100(s-c) = 100s - 100c$. Add $100c$: $Pc + 100c = 100s$. Divide by 100: $s = \dfrac{Pc+100c}{100} = \dfrac{c(P+100)}{100}$. Check with $P = 25$ and $c = 40$: $s = \dfrac{40 \times 125}{100} = 50$, and $\dfrac{100(50-40)}{40} = 25$.

commonErrors.feedback: Only part of the side was multiplied by $c$. Every term has to be multiplied: $Pc = 100s - 100c$, so the numerator carries $Pc$, not $P$.
The $100c$ went missing when the 100 was divided out. Adding $100c$ to both sides before dividing keeps it in the numerator, which is where the $c(P+100)$ comes from.

Scientific calculator (must be used)

context.setting: Pure algebra, no context, in the CCEA single-line format with the answer line reading a =

parts.stem:
$4a + 9b = ab$

Make $a$ the subject of the formula.
hints: $a$ appears in two terms, so collect those two terms on one side first.
Putting them on the right keeps the bracket positive: $ab - 4a = 9b$.
Factorise $a$ out, then divide by the whole bracket.
parts.workedSolution: Move $4a$ to the right and $9b$ to the left: $ab - 4a = 9b$. Both terms on the left contain $a$, so factorise: $a(b-4) = 9b$. Divide by $(b-4)$: $a = \dfrac{9b}{b-4}$. Check with $b = 6$: $a = \dfrac{54}{2} = 27$, and $4(27) + 9(6) = 162$ while $27 \times 6 = 162$.

commonErrors.feedback: Dividing by $b$ before collecting leaves an $a$ on each side, so nothing has been isolated. The first mark is for getting both $a$ terms onto the same side; over a third of the summer 2025 entry never did that.
The bracket has been broken up. $(b-4)$ is one factor, so the whole of it goes underneath the $9b$ in a single fraction.
The bracket is the right size but the wrong way round. Collecting on the right gives $ab - 4a$, which factorises to $a(b-4)$. Substituting $b = 6$ gives $-27$ here, and the formula needs $27$.

figures.alt: A solid cylinder standing on its circular base. A dashed line from the centre of the top circle to its edge is labelled r, and a double-headed arrow beside the cylinder marks its height h. The diagram is not drawn accurately.

parts.stem:
The total surface area of the solid cylinder in the diagram is $S = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi rh$.

Make $h$ the subject of the formula.
hints: Only one term contains $h$, so move the other one out of the way first.
$S - 2\pi r^2 = 2\pi rh$.
Divide the whole of the left-hand side by $2\pi r$, keeping it as one fraction.
parts.workedSolution: Subtract $2\pi r^2$ from both sides: $S - 2\pi r^2 = 2\pi rh$. Divide both sides by $2\pi r$: $h = \dfrac{S - 2\pi r^2}{2\pi r}$. Cancelling gives the equivalent form $h = \dfrac{S}{2\pi r} - r$, which is also accepted.

commonErrors.feedback: The $2\pi r^2$ was taken off after the division instead of before it, so it never got divided. Subtract it first, then divide the whole numerator.
The division by $2\pi r$ is missing. $h$ is multiplied by $2\pi r$ in the formula, so that factor has to come off before $h$ is alone.

parts.stem:
A cylinder has total surface area $340$ cm$^2$ and radius $4$ cm.

Work out its height.
Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.

scheme.for: substitutes $S = 340$ and $r = 4$ into a rearranged formula

hints: Work out $2\pi r^2$ first: $2\pi \times 16$.
Divide by $2\pi \times 4 = 25.13\ldots$
parts.workedSolution: $2\pi(4^2) = 100.530\ldots$, so the numerator is $340 - 100.530\ldots = 239.469\ldots$. The denominator is $2\pi(4) = 25.132\ldots$. Dividing gives $9.5281\ldots$, which is $9.5$ cm to 1 decimal place. Keep the long decimals in the calculator and round only on the answer line.

commonErrors.feedback: This comes from dividing 340 by $2\pi r$ and subtracting nothing, or subtracting after dividing. The $2\pi r^2$ has to come off the 340 before the division.
The value is right; the question asked for 1 decimal place, so the answer line needs $9.5$. Full accuracy in the working, stated accuracy on the line.

context.setting: A swinging pendulum, with the model formula given in the stem

figures.alt: A pendulum hanging from a fixed point on a hatched ceiling. The string, labelled L, is drawn swung out to the right with a round bob at its end, and a dashed arc shows the path of the swing. One full swing takes T seconds.

parts.stem:
The time $T$ seconds for one full swing of the pendulum in the diagram is modelled by $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}$, where $L$ metres is the length of the string and $g$ is a constant.

Make $L$ the subject of the formula.
hints: Divide both sides by $2\pi$ before you square anything.
Squaring both sides squares the whole of each side: $\dfrac{T^2}{4\pi^2} = \dfrac{L}{g}$.
Now multiply both sides by $g$.
parts.workedSolution: Divide both sides by $2\pi$: $\dfrac{T}{2\pi} = \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}$. Square both sides, remembering that $(2\pi)^2 = 4\pi^2$: $\dfrac{T^2}{4\pi^2} = \dfrac{L}{g}$. Multiply by $g$: $L = \dfrac{gT^2}{4\pi^2}$.

commonErrors.feedback: The $2\pi$ was divided out after the squaring, so it was never squared. Squaring $\dfrac{T}{2\pi}$ gives $\dfrac{T^2}{4\pi^2}$, not $\dfrac{T^2}{2\pi}$.
The right-hand side was squared but the $T$ was not. Squaring acts on the whole of both sides, so $T$ becomes $T^2$.

parts.stem:
Work out the length of a pendulum that takes $3$ seconds for one full swing.
Take $g = 10$.
Give your answer in metres correct to 2 decimal places.

scheme.for: substitutes $T = 3$ and $g = 10$ into a rearranged formula, e.g. $\dfrac{10 \times 9}{4\pi^2}$

hints: $\dfrac{10 \times 9}{4\pi^2} = \dfrac{90}{39.478\ldots}$
Round only at the end.
parts.workedSolution: $L = \dfrac{10(3^2)}{4\pi^2} = \dfrac{90}{39.4784\ldots} = 2.2797\ldots$, which is $2.28$ m to 2 decimal places. A one-metre pendulum swings in about two seconds, so a little over two metres for three seconds is a sensible size.

commonErrors.feedback: This comes from using $T$ rather than $T^2$. Square the 3 before dividing.
The value is right; 2 decimal places were asked for, so write $2.28$ on the answer line and keep the long version in your working.

resources: Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the paper
Scientific calculator (must be used)

context.setting: Pure algebra, no context; the subject appears twice and is squared

parts.stem:
$y = \dfrac{5x^2}{x^2 - 3}$

Show that $x^2 = \dfrac{3y}{y - 5}$.

scheme.examinerNote: The printed result alone, with no rearrangement lines, scores nothing on a Show that.

hints: Multiply both sides by $(x^2-3)$ and expand.
Treat $x^2$ as the thing you are making the subject, and collect the two $x^2$ terms together.
Factorise $x^2$ out, then divide by the bracket.
parts.workedSolution: Multiply both sides by $(x^2-3)$: $y(x^2-3) = 5x^2$, so $yx^2 - 3y = 5x^2$. Collect the $x^2$ terms: $yx^2 - 5x^2 = 3y$. Factorise: $x^2(y-5) = 3y$. Divide by $(y-5)$: $x^2 = \dfrac{3y}{y-5}$, which is the printed result. Every line is one of the three marks, so none of them can be skipped.

commonErrors.feedback: Dividing by $x^2$ or by $y$ before collecting leaves an $x^2$ on both sides, so nothing has been isolated. The first mark is for clearing the denominator and the second for gathering the two $x^2$ terms; over a third of the summer 2025 entry never reached that second line.

The bracket came out the wrong way round. Collecting on the left gives $yx^2 - 5x^2 = 3y$, which factorises to $x^2(y-5)$. Putting $y = 8$ into each version gives 8 and $-8$, and a squared quantity cannot be negative.
The collecting is done and it earns its mark. The next line takes $x^2$ outside a bracket: $x^2(y-5) = 3y$.

parts.stem:
Hence work out the positive value of $x$ when $y = 8$.
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
hints: Put $y = 8$ into the result from part (a).
Root it, and keep only the positive value because the question says so.
parts.workedSolution: $x^2 = \dfrac{3(8)}{8-5} = \dfrac{24}{3} = 8$, so $x = \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2} = 2.8284\ldots$, which is $2.83$ to 3 significant figures. Check: $\dfrac{5 \times 8}{8-3} = 8$, which is the $y$ you were given.

commonErrors.feedback: The 8 was halved rather than rooted. $x^2 = 8$ gives $x = \sqrt{8}$, which is about 2.83.
That is the other square root. The question asked for the positive value, so the answer line takes $2.83$.

findTheMistake.stem: Orla was asked: make $x$ the subject of $6x = wx + 15$. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: A term was moved, but the wrong one. Taking the 15 across leaves $x$ on both sides, and the last line proves it: the answer still contains an $x$, so $x$ has not been made the subject of anything. The move the mark is for is bringing the two $x$ terms together.
findTheMistake.feedback: Nothing here is careless — the algebra in each line is sound, it is just aimed at the wrong term. Before writing anything, underline every term containing the subject; here that is $6x$ and $wx$, and they have to end up side by side. Examiners in summer 2025 reported that over a third of candidates never made that move, which is why so few of the three marks were taken. Check yours with $w = 1$: the answer $\dfrac{15}{6-1} = 3$, and $6(3) = 18 = 1(3) + 15$.

findTheMistake.stem: Jack was asked: make $r$ the subject of $B = Ar^2 + 5$, where $r$ is positive. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The root was taken while $r^2$ was still multiplied by $A$. Rooting both sides of $B - 5 = Ar^2$ gives $\sqrt{B-5} = \sqrt{A}\,r$, not $Ar$, because the root acts on the whole of that side. Divide by $A$ first, and then the only thing left under the root is what belongs there.
findTheMistake.feedback: The first line of working is right and it keeps its mark, so this is a script that scores something rather than nothing. The rule to carry away is that a power comes off last: isolate $r^2$ completely, then root the whole of the other side. November 2024 examiners saw exactly this, together with root signs drawn over a numerator only. Test it with $A = 4$ and $B = 21$: the right answer gives $r = \sqrt{4} = 2$, and $4(2^2) + 5 = 21$.

findTheMistake.stem: Ellen was asked: rearrange $p - 5n = q$ to make $n$ the subject. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Two steps were done in one line and a sign was lost on the way. The $5n$ is being subtracted, so it moves across as $+5n$ and the $q$ comes back the other way: $p - q = 5n$. Written as $\dfrac{q-p}{5}$ the answer is the negative of the right one.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two things would have saved this. First, write the middle line: summer 2023 examiners noted that a mark was available for the intermediate line by itself, and jumping straight to the answer threw it away along with the accuracy mark. Second, substitute: with $p = 17$ and $q = 2$ the correct answer gives $n = 3$, and $17 - 5(3) = 2$, while this version gives $-3$. Thirty seconds of checking, two marks back.

prompts.prompt: The subject appears in two terms. Name the three moves, in order.
prompts.answer: Collect every term containing the subject on one side; factorise the subject out of them; divide both sides by the whole bracket.

prompts.prompt: What is the rule for the order in which you undo operations?
prompts.answer: Undo them in reverse order: the last thing done to the subject is the first thing you take off, and each operation is applied to the whole of both sides.

prompts.prompt: You have reached $r^2 = \dfrac{B-5}{A}$. Where exactly does the square root go?
prompts.answer: Over the whole of the other side: $r = \sqrt{\dfrac{B-5}{A}}$. It is not $\dfrac{\sqrt{B-5}}{A}$, and it is never shared out term by term.

prompts.prompt: Make $r$ the subject of $A = \pi r^2$, and say which sign you keep.
prompts.answer: $r = \sqrt{\dfrac{A}{\pi}}$. Divide by $\pi$ first, then root the whole fraction. Only the positive root is kept, because $r$ is a radius, and that reason is written down.

prompts.prompt: The subject is inside a denominator. What is the first move, and what do you multiply?
prompts.answer: Clear the fraction: multiply every term on both sides by the denominator. Only then can the subject be collected and factorised.

prompts.prompt: You have reached $x(8-w) = 12+3w$. What do you divide by, and what must you not divide by?
prompts.answer: Divide by the whole bracket $(8-w)$, which goes underneath in one piece. Not by 8 alone, not by $-w$ alone, and never cancel a term that is not a factor.

prompts.prompt: How do you check a rearrangement in under a minute?
prompts.answer: Pick easy values for the other letters, work the subject out from your answer, then put every value back into the original formula and check the two sides agree.

prompts.prompt: What exactly does 'make $x$ the subject' ask you to produce?
prompts.answer: A formula of the form $x = \ldots$, with $x$ alone on one side and appearing nowhere on the other. If an $x$ is still visible on the right, the question has not been answered.
keyWords: x nowhere on the other side

prompts.prompt: You are out of time on a three-mark rearrangement. What is worth writing down?
prompts.answer: The collected line, and then the factorised line. Each scores on its own, and CCEA reported a mark sitting on the intermediate line even where nothing was finished.

prompts.prompt: The volume of a cone is $V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$. Make $h$ the subject, then make $r$ the subject.
prompts.answer: $h = \dfrac{3V}{\pi r^2}$, which takes two steps. $r = \sqrt{\dfrac{3V}{\pi h}}$, which takes the same two steps and then a root over the whole fraction, positive because $r$ is a radius.

insight.ruleToRemember: Collect every term containing the subject on one side, factorise the subject out, divide by the bracket; undo powers last, applying the root to the whole side.
